Abstract.
[id=abstract1.1] Scaling training data and model parameters has long driven progress in large language models (LLMs), but this paradigm is increasingly constrained by the scarcity of high-quality data and diminishing returns from rising computational costs. As a result, recent work is increasing the focus on continual learning from real-world deployment, where user interaction logs provide a rich source of authentic human feedback and procedural knowledge.
However, learning from user logs is challenging due to their unstructured and noisy nature. Vanilla LLM systems often struggle to distinguish useful feedback signals from noisy user behavior, and the disparity between user log collection and model optimization (e.g., the off-policy optimization problem) further strengthens the problem. To this end, we propose UNO (User log-driveN Optimization), a unified framework for improving LLM systems (LLMsys) with user logs. UNO first distills logs into semi-structured rules and preference pairs, then employs query-and-feedback-driven clustering to manage data heterogeneity, and finally quantifies the cognitive gap between the model’s prior knowledge and the log data. This assessment guides the LLMsys to adaptively filter out noisy feedback and construct different modules for primary and reflective experiences extracted from user logs, thereby improving future responses. Extensive experiments show that UNO achieves state-of-the-art effectiveness and efficiency, significantly outperforming Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) and memory-based baselines. 11

[id=S1]
1. Introduction
[id=S1.p1.1] In recent years, the development of large language models (LLMs) has largely followed scaling laws, in which scaling training data and model parameters yields predictable capability gains (Kaplan et al., 2020; Fang et al., 2024). However, this line of progress is increasingly constrained as high-quality training data are becoming increasingly scarce, and the marginal performance gains from model scaling are diminishing relative to the rapidly rising computational costs (Villalobos et al., 2024).
These challenges motivate a growing interest in moving beyond static, pre-trained models toward more dynamic systems that can adapt by continually acquiring new supervision signals through real-world interaction (Shi et al., 2025a; Zheng et al., 2025).
[id=S1.p2.1] In information retrieval, a well-established paradigm for addressing the above challenges in search engines and recommendation systems is to collect and exploit user logs to continually improve system performance (Zhang et al., 2019; Croft et al., 2010). By learning from implicit feedback, such as click behavior, these systems can construct automatic self-improving loops without reliance on human supervision. Similarly, deployed LLMs continuously accumulate user logs (e.g., prompts, model outputs, and user revisions or feedback) that provide large-scale, authentic feedback on model behavior across tasks, as well as extensive procedural memories generated under user guidance. These logs represent a rich but underexplored resource for the optimization of LLM-based systems (LLMsys) (Ai et al., 2025).
[id=S1.p3.1] Despite these successes in classical IR systems, continual learning from user logs remains particularly challenging for LLM-based systems due to several fundamental differences. First, user feedback for LLMs is sparse and unstructured compared to conventional labeled data or click behaviors in IR systems, making it difficult to extract useful feedback signals.
For example, classic IR systems provide results in a list, and it’s straightforward to collect fine-grained feedback when the user clicks on each result (Joachims, 2002; Kelly and Teevan, 2003). LLMsys, on the other hand, provides responses in free-form text, and users either directly get the answers from the response without interacting with it or only provide coarse-grained verbal or action feedback (e.g., copy) to the response as a whole.
Our preliminary study shows that LLMs struggle to distinguish useful knowledge and feedback from noisy signals in user logs, which we refer to as the Signal-or-Noise Dilemma. 22
2
We describe this in detail in Section 3.3.3.
Second, in contrast to search or recommendation systems, where information and knowledge are explicitly stored outside the retrieval model, LLMs entangle knowledge and reasoning implicitly within their parameters (Su et al., 2025b).
Learning new abilities autonomously while preventing catastrophic forgetting in the parameter space has been widely considered a fundamental challenge for LLMs (Gao et al., 2025).
Last but not least, user logs are collected from product systems, which may differ from the target model to be optimized or under optimization.
Such off-policy optimization problems are common in IR systems, but are particularly challenging for LLMs because of their huge parameter size and black-box nature (Levine et al., 2020).
[id=S1.p4.1] To address these challenges, we introduce UNO (User log-driveN Optimization), a framework for continual LLM evolution from user logs. UNO has two stages: (i) learning experience modules from logs and (ii) retrieving and applying modules at inference time.
In the learning stage, UNO constructs multiple experience modules from the collected user logs, each implemented as a specialized adapter functioning either as an expert for direct generation or a critic for iterative refinement.
In the inference stage, UNO retrieves relevant experience modules given the current user query or task context and composes them with the base LLM to generate enhanced responses.
Specifically, for each user session, UNO uses an LLM to extract a semi-structured rule set from the feedback signal (e.g., user comments or corrections), which tell the models how to improve the response. 33
3
A rule set consists of actionable editing guidelines distilled from unstructured user logs, specifying how to refine the LLM’s original responses. See Section 3.3.1 for details.
It then generates a revised response following the extracted rules and forms a preference pair by contrasting the original response with the revised one.
Then it conducts agglomerative clustering (Müllner, 2011) based on each session’s query and extracted rule sets to divide the user logs into multiple clusters.
Inspired by John Dewey’s philosophy on Experience and Nature (Dewey, 2012), we develop two types of modules, i.e., a primary experience module and a reflective experience module, to update the knowledge of LLMsys.
The primary experience module learns a parameter-efficient adapter (e.g., LoRA (Hu et al., 2022)) from the data in a cluster directly and can be activated in the inference stage.
The reflective experience module learns a critic adapter that critiques a draft response and provides actionable revision suggestions, enabling an iterative refine-and-regenerate loop.
At inference time, it does not modify the weights of the base model.
Instead, it offers suggestions based on the tasks and the original LLM responses so that the LLMsys could revise and regenerate better responses.
[id=S1.p5.1] To determine which types of experience module to use for each cluster, we define cognitive gap to measure how well the experience extracted from user logs matches the original LLM’s understanding of the queries and tasks in each cluster.
If the cognitive gap is small and the performance of the primary experience module trained on the cluster is satisfactory, we treat the cluster as a primary experience cluster. Otherwise, we treat the cluster as a reflective experience cluster.
Furthermore, since user logs are collected under historical system policies and may not reflect the current deployment distribution, UNO mitigates off-policy risks by avoiding direct updates to the base model and instead relying on module-level adaptation with verification/critique.
In the reflective experience clusters, user logs are used to construct the critic models that provide suggestions instead of directly changing the parameters of LLMs.
In the primary experience clusters, we design a simulated performance verifier by using an LLM-as-Judge paradigm (Li et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025a) with the extracted rules from user logs as context to evaluate the primary experience module (i.e., the LoRA learned directly from user logs).
If the verifier determines that the primary experience module is not good enough, the cluster would be re-tagged as a reflective experience cluster and a reflective experience module would be built instead.
[id=S1.p6.1] We evaluate the methods on MemoryBench (Ai et al., 2025), a comprehensive continual learning benchmark covering multiple datasets, domains, tasks, and languages, which offers scalable user logs and corresponding evaluation tasks. We compare UNO with conventional training approaches, Retrieval-Augmented-Generation (RAG) (Lewis et al., 2020), and memory-based methods, and UNO demonstrates state-of-the-art performance in both effectiveness and efficiency.
[id=S1.p7.1] To summarize, our contributions are as follows:
[id=S1.I1.i1] •
[id=S1.I1.i1.p1.1] We conduct, as far as we know, the first study on the optimization of LLMsys capabilities using user logs and characterize several challenges, including the Signal–or-Noise Dilemma.
[id=S1.I1.i2] •
[id=S1.I1.i2.p1.1] We propose UNO, a novel framework for LLMsys continual learning from user logs. It features a cluster-based multiple experience management system constructed based on the cognitive gap between the model and log data.
[id=S1.I1.i3] •
[id=S1.I1.i3.p1.1] Extensive experiments on continual learning benchmarks show that UNO achieves state-of-the-art performance across diverse tasks and languages, significantly outperforming Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) and memory-based baselines in both effectiveness and efficiency.
[id=S2]
2. Related Work
[id=S2.SS1]
2.1. Memory for LLM Systems
[id=S2.SS1.p1.1] Research on LLM memory has progressed from simple retrieval-augmented pipelines to complex management systems (Hu et al., 2025). Representative approaches include hierarchical memory architectures for history management (MemoryOS (Kang et al., 2025)), graph-based storage (Mem0 (Chhikara et al., 2025)), and self-organizing mechanisms for efficient information linking (A-Mem (Xu et al., 2025)). Correspondingly, benchmarks such as LoCoMo (Maharana et al., 2024) evaluate long-range reasoning and conversational coherence. A key distinction between these works and ours lies in data granularity.
Existing memory systems operate at the user level, aiming to adapt LLMs to individual preferences or personalized knowledge, and are evaluated on question answering or reasoning grounded in a single user’s interaction history. In contrast, we focus on system-wide user logs, aggregating feedback from a diverse user population to drive the continual learning of a deployed system’s knowledge and capabilities, and evaluate performance on entirely new online requests rather than over historical logs.
[id=S2.SS2]
2.2. Evolutionary Agent Frameworks
[id=S2.SS2.p1.1] Continual learning (Shi et al., 2025b) aims to enable LLMsys to incrementally acquire new skills without retraining from scratch. Within this paradigm, evolutionary agent frameworks (Zhai et al., 2025; Feng et al., 2025) represent a main direction, focusing on self-evolution during deployment through sustained agent–environment interaction and feedback.
AlphaEvolve (Novikov et al., 2025) demonstrates that LLMs can iteratively improve their performance on complex tasks through evolutionary processes. More recent approaches further integrate memory into evolutionary LLMsys. For instance, MemRL (Zhang et al., 2026) leverages reinforcement learning to optimize memory usage based on continuous environmental interaction.
Despite their effectiveness, these evolutionary systems rely heavily on explicit reward signals repeatedly provided by the environment (e.g., code executors) to drive self-evolution for the same task. In contrast, our work optimizes LLMs using user logs. This setting reflects real-world conditions, where users are not instructed to act as annotators and systems cannot assume repeated labeling of identical queries. Moreover, reward signals in user logs are typically implicit, posing additional challenges for continual learning.
[id=S2.SS3]
2.3. User Log-driven Optimization Paradigms
[id=S2.SS3.p1.1] User log–based optimization has a long history in recommender systems and search engines, where interaction data underpin ranking learning (Zhang et al., 2019; Croft et al., 2010). However, in the LLM domain, this paradigm is relatively new, as conventional training mainly depends on high-quality datasets. Recently, researchers begin to investigate the potential of user logs for optimizing LLMs on specific tasks. Yin et al. leverage user click data to improve query suggestion in conversational systems (Yin et al., 2025), while Han et al. enhance emotional support capabilities by mining user feedback actions from production environments (Han et al., 2025). While these approaches demonstrate the value of user logs, they are limited to particular behavioral signals and narrow task settings. In contrast, our work introduces a fundamentally new paradigm, where LLMsys can learn directly from raw user dialogue logs, enabling systematic capability improvement.
[id=S3]
3. Methodology
[id=S3.p1.1] In this section, we describe the UNO (User log-driveN Optimization) framework in detail. UNO aims to enable autonomous, continual learning for LLMs by leveraging raw user logs. We first introduce the task and define the notations, then provide an overview of UNO, and finally describe the complete workflow, including preprocessing, training, and test-time generation.
[id=S3.SS1]
3.1. Problem Formulation and Preliminaries
[id=S3.SS1.p1.1] Let πθ\pi_{\theta} denote a base LLM policy with parameters θ\theta. User logs are represented as a set of sessions 𝒟={S1,S2,…,SN}\mathcal{D}=\{S_{1},S_{2},\dots,S_{N}\}, where each session Si=(qi,yi,ℱi)S_{i}=(q_{i},y_{i},\mathcal{F}_{i}) comprises a user query qiq_{i}, an initial response yi∼πθ(⋅∣qi)y_{i}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid q_{i}), and a subsequent interaction trajectory ℱi\mathcal{F}_{i}. The interaction trajectory ℱi={(ui,t,ri,t)}t=1Ti\mathcal{F}_{i}=\{(u_{i,t},r_{i,t})\}_{t=1}^{T_{i}} consists of Ti≥0T_{i}\geq 0 dialogue turns, where ui,tu_{i,t} denotes the user input and ri,tr_{i,t} denotes the corresponding LLM response. In real user logs, such trajectories may reflect explicit corrections or implicit preferences from users, but they may also contain irrelevant noise or be empty (i.e., Ti=0T_{i}=0).
[id=S3.SS1.p2.1] The goal is to exploit 𝒟\mathcal{D} to drive the system from the initial policy πθ\pi_{\theta} toward an improved policy π′\pi^{\prime}. During testing, given a new query qt​e​s​tq_{test}, the system produces a response yy, i.e., y∼π′(⋅∣qt​e​s​t)y\sim\pi^{\prime}(\cdot\mid q_{test}). Successful optimization requires that

[id=S3.SS1.p2.2] where 𝒱\mathcal{V} denotes a response quality metric. Note that user logs may contain either high-value signals or noise, which requires an optimization framework to exhibit two core capabilities: 1) Positive Adaptivity, whereby the system can convert valuable signals into improvements in model capability; and (2) Noise Robustness, whereby the system maintains stable performance without degradation when exposed to low-quality or noisy logs.
[id=S3.SS1.p3.1] Although not originally designed for this task, several existing approaches can be adapted.
Traditional full fine-tuning updates model parameters to θ′\theta^{\prime} to directly fit the log distribution, yielding πF​T(⋅∣qi)=πθ′(⋅∣qi)\pi_{FT}(\cdot\mid q_{i})=\pi_{\theta^{\prime}}(\cdot\mid q_{i}). [id=S3.SS2]
3.2. Overview of UNO
Figure 1. The workflow of UNO. UNO first distills and filters raw user logs, then performs clustering and a cognitive gap assessment to select the type of experience module (primary or reflective). At inference time, UNO identifies the appropriate cluster and applies an inference strategy aligned with the type of that cluster.
[id=S3.SS2.p1.1] UNO is the first optimization framework for LLMsys specifically built on user logs, enabling LLMsys to continuously and adaptively evolve while keeping noise robustness. UNO consists of four stages: 1) Preprocessing: it filters and distills noisy user logs to construct a preference dataset. It then partitions the data and assesses how well the LLM accepts user feedback, which is used to estimate the difficulty of optimization. Guided by these signals, the framework constructs either Primary Experience Module or Reflective Experience Module for different clusters, which is inspired by John Dewey’s philosophy on Experience and Nature (Dewey, 2012). The former trains an Expert LoRA to directly produce answers at inference time, while the latter trains a Critic LoRA that offers guidance on the base LLM’s initial response during inference. For Primary Experience Module, we further use the distilled rule sets to build a simulated performance verifier to evaluate the trained LoRAs and ensure their quality before deployment. Finally, at 4) Inference Workflow, for a new query, UNO first matches it to the nearest cluster. If the cluster has a primary experience module, the corresponding Expert LoRA is directly loaded to produce the answer. If it is based on reflective experience, the base LLM first generates an initial answer. The Critic LoRA then provides feedback based on this output, and the base LLM revises the answer according to the feedback. Figure 1 provides an overview of the complete workflow of UNO, while Algorithm 1 presents the pseudocode for the training process. 44

[id=S3.SS3]
3.3. Preprocessing
[id=S3.SS3.SSS1]
3.3.1. Raw User Log Filtering and Distillation
[id=S3.SS3.SSS1.p1.1] Raw user logs consist of unstructured text and may contain noisy or meaningless user inputs (Ai et al., 2025). We utilize the LLM to preprocess these logs by filtering meaningless content and converting the rest into semi-structured rule sets.
Specifically, for each dialogue session (qi,yi,ℱi)(q_{i},y_{i},\mathcal{F}_{i}), we first discard samples with empty ℱi\mathcal{F}_{i}. The base LLM is prompted to perform feedback filtering and distillation, transforming unstructured user responses into an explicit semi-structured rule set ℛi={ri,1,ri,2,…,ri,k}\mathcal{R}_{i}=\{r_{i,1},r_{i,2},\dots,r_{i,k}\}.
For example, a user submits an academic paper and requests a report written in a journalistic style. Regarding the LLM’s response, the user complains that the language is too technical and that the readers cannot understand the social impact of the technology. The rule set distilled by the LLM based on this interaction is as follows:
1) Use accessible, non-technical language in a news style;
2) Emphasize the technology’s real-world impact and relevance.
[id=S3.SS3.SSS1.p2.1] Then, we remove the items with empty rule sets, which indicates that the dialogues are uninformative.
Subsequently, the LLM is guided to revise the original response yiy_{i} under the constraints imposed by ℛi\mathcal{R}_{i}, yielding a better response yiw∼πθ(⋅∣qi,ℛi,yi)y_{i}^{w}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid q_{i},\mathcal{R}_{i},y_{i}). This process constructs a preference pair (qi,yiw,yil)(q_{i},y_{i}^{w},y_{i}^{l}), where yil=yiy_{i}^{l}=y_{i}.
[id=S3.SS3.SSS2]
3.3.2. Dual-feature Data Clustering.
[id=S3.SS3.SSS2.p1.1] To facilitate training and allow for more precise assessment of noise risk, we construct a vector
[id=S3.Ex2]
vi=[Norm​(E⁡(qi))⊕Norm​(E⁡(ℛi))],v_{i}=[\text{Norm}(E(q_{i}))\oplus\text{Norm}(E(\mathcal{R}_{i}))],
[id=S3.SS3.SSS2.p2.1] where E⁡(⋅)E(\cdot) represents a sentence encoder and ⊕\oplus denotes vector concatenation. We employ hierarchical agglomerative clustering using Ward’s linkage (Müllner, 2011), which iteratively merges the pair of clusters that results in the smallest increase in total intra-cluster variance.
The merging process continues until the Ward objective increment (i.e., the increase in intra-cluster variance) exceeds a threshold ϵv​a​r\epsilon_{var}, producing the final set of clusters 𝒞\mathcal{C}. In our implementation, we set ϵv​a​r\epsilon_{var} to 4 (Section 4.3).
This ensures that samples in each cluster are highly aligned in both semantic intent and applicable rules, thereby lowering the complexity of model training.
[id=S3.SS3.SSS3]
3.3.3. Cognitive Gap Assessment
[id=S3.SS3.SSS3.Px1]
Signal-or-Noise Dilemma.
[id=S3.SS3.SSS3.Px1.p1.1] The central challenge in exploiting user logs for model optimization is determining whether the logs truly contribute to improvement.
The distillation stage uses the LLM to filter out noise, but the LLM itself may be unreliable.
Once incoming data exceeds its current knowledge or capability boundary, self-filtering may fail.
When signals in user logs differ substantially from the model’s cognition, two interpretations are possible: (1) the data may encode previously unmastered but valuable hard knowledge; or (2) feedback may be dominated by noise or user bias, and indiscriminate internalization can harm performance. A self-improving system cannot theoretically distinguish between these two cases, giving rise to the Signal-or-Noise Dilemma.
[id=S3.SS3.SSS3.Px1.p2.1] To address this, we introduce a quantitative notion of cognitive gap. It not only reflects task difficulty but also facilitates identifying potentially high-risk noise within the clusters.
[id=S3.SS3.SSS3.Px1.p3.1] Assessment Process.
We quantify the cognitive gap through three steps: 1) Rule Prediction: For each query qiq_{i} in cluster 𝒞k\mathcal{C}_{k}, the base model πθ\pi_{\theta} independently generates the rule set ℛiL​L​M\mathcal{R}_{i}^{LLM} without access to user logs.
2) Gap Quantification: A pre-trained reranker computes the semantic distance between the predicted rules ℛiL​L​M\mathcal{R}_{i}^{LLM} and the distilled rules ℛi\mathcal{R}_{i}, yielding a cognitive gap score gi=Dist​(ℛiL​L​M,ℛi)∈[0,1]g_{i}=\text{Dist}(\mathcal{R}_{i}^{LLM},\mathcal{R}_{i})\in[0,1].
3) Cluster-level Profiling: We calculate the average gap μk=1|𝒞k|​∑i∈𝒞kgi\mu_{k}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{C}_{k}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{C}_{k}}g_{i} for each cluster. Based on the value of μk\mu_{k} and a predefined threshold τ∗\tau^{*}, clusters are classified as “Low-Gap” or “High-Gap”.
[id=S3.SS3.SSS3.Px1.p4.1] Theoretical Framework of Cognitive Gap.
We formalize the cognitive gap to provide a theoretical basis for evaluating optimization risk. Let HH denote high-quality data and NN noisy data, with priors P⁡(H)=αP(H)=\alpha and P⁡(N)=1−αP(N)=1-\alpha. The core intuition lies in the LLM’s noise discrimination capability across different cognitive regions. In low-gap regions, high-quality data typically represent minor refinements of the model’s existing cognition and are largely aligned with it, whereas noisy data are inherently random and statistically unlikely to exhibit such alignment, making the two highly separable. In contrast, high-gap regions contain samples that deviate substantially from the model’s current knowledge and capabilities. Under these conditions, an LLM cannot reliably distinguish “informative novel signals” from “uninformative random noise,” causing their distributions to become increasingly similar from the LLM’s cognitive perspective. We formalize this with the following assumption:

Next, we illustrate how clustering concentrates the cognitive gaps within each cluster, enabling the emergence of clearly defined low- and high-gap clusters. This property allows us to adaptively select the optimization strategy.
Assumption 3.3.
